content: Human T-lymphotropic viruses, type I (HTLV-I) and type II (HTLV-II), are retroviruses that infect humans. They are distinct from the human immunodeficiency viruses (HIV-1 and HIV-2), which cause AIDS. HTLV-I and HTLV-II belong to the oncovirus subfamily of retroviruses and are capable of transforming human lymphocytes into self-sustaining cells in vitro. Infections with these viruses are typically detected through serologic testing, which identifies the presence of antibodies to HTLV-I or HTLV-II, indicating infection. In 1988, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) recommended screening the blood supply for HTLV-I, and since then, all blood donations in the United States have been tested for antibodies to HTLV-I. However, the screening tests, which use HTLV-I antigens, cannot reliably distinguish between HTLV-I and HTLV-II infections. Approximately 2,000 HTLV-I/II-infected blood donors were identified in the first year of screening, with polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing revealing that about half were infected with HTLV-I and the other half with HTLV-II. These donors are permanently deferred from donating blood and are counseled about their infections. HTLV-I infection is endemic in regions such as southwestern Japan, the Caribbean, Melanesia, and parts of Africa. In these areas, prevalence rates can reach as high as 15% in the general population. In the United States, the seroprevalence of HTLV-I/II among blood donors is approximately 0.016%. HTLV-I is primarily transmitted from mother to child through breastfeeding, by sexual contact, blood transfusion, or sharing contaminated needles. Mother-to-child transmission occurs in about 25% of breastfed infants born to HTLV-I-seropositive mothers. Sexual transmission is more efficient from males to females, with studies showing a 60.8% transmission rate over 10 years in married couples in Japan. Blood transfusion involving cellular components, such as whole blood or platelets, can also transmit HTLV-I, with seroconversion rates of 44% to 63% in endemic areas. HTLV-I is associated with two major diseases: adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATL) and HTLV-I-associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paraparesis (HAM/TSP). ATL is a malignancy of HTLV-I-infected CD4+ T-lymphocytes and is characterized by circulating abnormal lymphocytes (flower cells), lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, skin lesions, hypercalcemia, and lytic bone lesions. Median survival for ATL patients is 11 months, and conventional chemotherapy is not curative. HAM/TSP is a chronic, progressive neurologic disease characterized by spastic paraparesis, lower limb weakness, sensory disturbances, and urinary incontinence. It affects less than 1% of HTLV-I-infected individuals and is believed to be immunologically mediated. HTLV-II, on the other hand, is prevalent among injecting drug users in the United States and Europe and is also found in some indigenous populations in the Americas. HTLV-II is transmitted similarly to HTLV-I, but much less is known about its specific modes and efficiency of transmission. Unlike HTLV-I, HTLV-II has not been definitively associated with any specific diseases, although rare cases of HAM/TSP-like illnesses and other conditions have been reported. Serologic testing for HTLV-I and HTLV-II involves enzyme immunoassays, Western immunoblot, and radioimmunoprecipitation assays. These tests are used to confirm the presence of antibodies to HTLV-I/II and to differentiate between the two viruses. Blood donors who test positive for HTLV-I/II are notified and permanently deferred from donating blood. Counseling for HTLV-Ior HTLV-II-infected individuals includes advice on preventing transmission, such as avoiding blood or tissue donation, refraining from breastfeeding, and using barrier precautions during sexual activity. For individuals with HIV and CD4+ T-lymphocyte counts below 100 cells/µL, prophylaxis against Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) is recommended. Rifabutin, at a dose of 300 mg daily, is the preferred prophylactic agent. Disseminated MAC is diagnosed through blood cultures and treated with a combination of at least two drugs, including azithromycin or clarithromycin. Therapy should continue for the patient’s lifetime if clinical and microbiologic improvement is observed. Monitoring of symptoms and blood cultures is essential during treatment. HIV-infected children are also at risk for disseminated MAC, and their diagnosis, therapy, and prophylaxis should follow similar guidelines to those for adults.
